hook.line: Someone you care about is upset, and you do not want to fix it, you want them to feel heard. Tomás needed this the day Vale found out about Altamira's offer. One small phrase does it.
hook.en: I understand that you're upset. (to a woman)

examples.es: Entiendo que estés molesta con ellos.
examples.en: I understand that you're upset with them. (to a woman)

examples.es: Comprendo que no quieras hablar ahora.
examples.en: I understand that you don't want to talk now. (to a friend)
I gather you're arriving tomorrow. (to a friend)
I understand that Tomás is nervous.

examples.es: Entiendo que no te guste el cambio.
examples.en: I understand that you don't like the change. (to a friend)
I gather they're coming on Monday.

rule:
Two meanings hide behind *entiendo que*.

With the plain verb, you have just taken in a fact: *Entiendo que llegas mañana*. Nothing more.

With the *-e* style verb (*estés, quieras, esté, tenga, te guste*), you are saying: it makes sense that you feel this. *Entiendo que estés molesta* means "I get why you're upset".

So the verb form carries the kindness. English uses a tone of voice; Spanish changes the ending. *Comprendo que* works the same way.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive after a verb of understanding: it presents the feeling as reasonable instead of reporting it as news.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose the right form and type the whole sentence (I understand why you're upset, to a woman): Entiendo que ___ molesta. (*estás* or *estés*)
yourTurn.why: You are saying her feeling makes sense, so the verb takes the *-és* ending, *estés*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (to a friend): I understand that you don't want to talk now.
yourTurn.answer: Comprendo que no quieras hablar ahora.
accept: Entiendo que no quieras hablar ahora.
yourTurn.why: Your friend's feeling is reasonable, so *quieras* and not *quieres*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (to a man): I understand why you're tired.
yourTurn.why: *Estés* shows you accept the feeling, and *cansado* matches a man.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (to a friend): I understand that you're arriving tomorrow. (just taking in the news)
yourTurn.why: This is only information, so the plain verb *llegas* stays.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about Vale: Entiendo que estés molesta.
Make it about you all, all men: Entiendo que estés molesto.
yourTurn.why: For *ustedes* the verb ends in *-én* and the adjective is plural.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (to a friend): I understand that you don't like the change.
yourTurn.answer: Entiendo que no te guste el cambio.
accept: Comprendo que no te guste el cambio.
yourTurn.why: A reasonable feeling again, so *guste* and not *gusta*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. The first only reports a fact; to say her feeling makes sense, change the ending to *estés*.
Plain news about what someone does stays in the plain form; the *-e* style is for feelings.

pitfalls.wrong: Entiendo que no te gusta el cambio.
pitfalls.right: Entiendo que no te guste el cambio.
pitfalls.why: To show you accept the feeling, *gusta* becomes *guste*.

personal: Think of someone who has been a bit down lately. Write one line to them with *Entiendo que* and a feeling.
